newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Utilities still seek promised Hungary profit.
newsitem.headline: Utilities still seek promised Hungary profit.

text.p: West European utilities Tractebel and Electricite de France have expressed dissatisfaction at the slow pace of talks with the Hungarian government aimed at resolving differences over its energy pricing mechanism.
"The negotiations are becoming glutinous," Tractebel's representative in Hungary Tibor Kuhl told Reuters.
"I can't tell you I'm very happy," he said, referring to agreements about the purchasing and pricing of power in the country's energy sector.
Tractebel purchased a 48 percent stake in the oil-fired Dunamenti power station in December 1995.
The Belgian holding company is currently negotiating with Hungary's state privatisation agency (APV) over the price it is to receive for power the plant supplies to Hungary's electricity company MVM.

Other western utilities such as Electricite de France (EDF), Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE bought large stakes in the energy distribution sector in late 1995 and were all promised an eight percent return on investment.

But they believe the government contravened the original sales agreements by cancelling planned price rises last October and by setting energy price rises in January that still did not secure the expected margins.

"We are continuing not to get the promised profit," said Pierre Abou, representative in Hungary of EDF, which has just under 50 percent stakes in two regional electricity distribution companies, Edasz and Demasz.
"The formula is still valid but we disagree on the implementation -- these are technical questions and this is the reason it's taking so long."

Tractebel announced in January it was preparing legal action against the Hungarian government to recover its $141 million investment after the cancellation of the October price rise. Kuhl said the company has still not ruled out the possibility.

"I can't exclude (court action)," he said. "It is about privatisation commitments and terms of reference as described in the offering memorandum which were not respected in October last year...but it is a different issue from what we are discussing now."

EDF's Abou said western utilities had been pushing since January for the inclusion in the energy pricing formula of costs such as environmental safeguards, insurance, social payments and depreciation but had failed to persuade Hungary's Energy Office (MEH) to incorporate any of them.
MEH announced a 3.6 percent quarterly price rise for April 1 which took into account only the devaluation of the forint in the first three months of the year.
Abou said he was looking for something more in the June 1 price adjustment and said EDF would reconsider its position on future investments if no progress had been made by then.
"If agreement is not reached before June we shall give them our precise standpoint," he said. "It is in our common interest to have this problem solved by the end of the quarter."

Kuhl also suggested a clearer picture on profitability was needed within the next few months. He said that by the third quarter Tractebel would determine whether its planned investment programme could go ahead.
"1997 is a test case on whether this investment is profitable or not." he said.
"(But) I'm not sure that the guaranteed return on equity will be achieved."

However, he said an agreement to allow Tractebel to pass on market price changes in heavy oil meant the company would not bear the huge losses incurred by the Dunamenti operation last year when it bought oil from Hungarian company MOL at market rates but sold electricity to MVM at a fixed price.
"The tariff structure in 1997 is much less unpredictable than was the case in 1996 so there is already the possibility for planning the year and forecasting a certain level of profit."

Under the new pricing mechanism the producer price continues to be set by the government, but an additional compensation fee -- which can be positive or negative depending on the movement of the market price for MOL oil -- was added, Kuhl said.
